title.title: Every $a/b$ is a short sum of unit fractions
title.subtitle: Claim: every $a/b$ is a sum of $O(\log\log b)$ distinct unit fractions, and that is best possible

beats.text: $N(b)$: the most distinct unit fractions some $a/b$ needs. Schematic, constants dropped
The claim: $\log\log b$, which matches the known lower bound

verify.detail: In Lean, with explicit constants such as $257/\log 2$
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean docs and allowed axioms; we did not build it

sources.quote: Erdos (1950) proved N(b) << log b/log log b and the lower bound order log log b
There are absolute c1, c2 with c1 log log b <= N(b) <= c2 log log b for b large
33 pages; denominators are unrestricted in size. Lean includes explicit constants like 257/log 2
only `propext`, `Quot.sound` and `Classical.choice` for every family here

plain: Write any fraction as a sum of different $1/n$ pieces, as ancient Egyptians did: very few pieces suffice

steps: Look at many candidate denominators at once
On average they have many divisors with small remainders
So good denominators exist: $\log\log b$ terms suffice

voice.text: How many unit fractions does a fraction need? Vose's bound stood since nineteen eighty-five.
Most denominators have many divisors with small remainders, so few terms suffice.
Claimed: log log b terms, the best possible.
